sections.h: Ezekiel's Temple: the laws of the house (44-46)
sections.b: After the glory returns (43:1-5), Ezekiel is told to learn the rules for entering, serving in and visiting the Temple: the shut east gate (44:1-3), the exclusion of foreigners (44:6-9), the priests' clothes and duties (44:17-31), the festival offerings (45:18-25) and the leader's worship (46:1-15). Many of them differ from the Torah, and since the Talmud (Shabbat 13b) this has been the main puzzle of the book. The readings are: a future Temple with sacrifices; the Church or Christ; an ideal blueprint; or a puzzle left to Elijah.

A stream rises under the Temple threshold, grows without tributaries, and heals the Dead Sea. It joins Eden's river (Genesis 2:10-14), Psalm 46:4, Joel 3:18 and Zechariah 14:8, and is taken up in John 7:37-39 and Revelation 22:1-2.
sections.refs: Ezekiel 47:1-12; Genesis 2:10-14; Psalm 46:4; Joel 3:18; Zechariah 14:8; John 7:37-39; Revelation 22:1-2

sections.b: The Temple sits in a strip of land set apart for the Zadokite priests, with a strip for the Levites and a smaller one for the city. The Hebrew totals (10,000 wide in 45:1 and 48:13) do not add up; Swete's Greek reads 20,000 in both, which fits, though its 20,000 for each strip in 45:3 and 45:5 does not. The leader's land lies on both sides.

common: Ezekiel's Temple was never built as described.
uncommon: A few readers think Ezekiel's rules describe an actual plan that the returning exiles were meant to build.

sections.h: The sons of Zadok in Ezekiel 44-48
sections.b: Ezekiel promotes the Levite priests of Zadok's line, who 'kept their charge' when Israel went astray (44:15; 48:11), and demotes the other Levites to gatekeepers and slaughterers (44:10-14). They alone come near the altar, wear linen in the inner court (44:17), judge disputes (44:24) and receive the best of the holy district (45:4; 48:10-12). The Damascus Document quotes 44:15 of the Qumran community.

Ezekiel 44:9-31 sets out the Zadokite priests' dress (linen only), hair, wine, marriage, contact with the dead, teaching and judging, and their food. The Levites are demoted because they served at idolatrous shrines. The LORD is the priests' only 'inheritance' (44:28), as in Numbers 18:20, but they get a holy district all the same (45:4; 48:10).

uncommon: Haran and Milgrom argue the priestly laws are older than Ezekiel, against Wellhausen's order.

sections.b: Ezekiel asks for a daily lamb in the morning, a bull, six lambs and a ram at the new moon, a bull for the leader and the people at Passover, and seven bulls and seven rams a day for the seven days of the festival. The numbers differ from Numbers 28-29. The leader pays for them from the people's contribution, but the priests offer them.

Ezekiel 44:6-9 bars uncircumcised foreigners from the sanctuary; 47:22-23 gives resident foreigners with children a share of the land among the tribes. The two verses address different groups: the first, uncircumcised outsiders working in the Temple, the second, foreigners who live among Israel. Isaiah 56:3-8 welcomes foreigners to the LORD's house.
The people give the leader a small portion of grain, oil and sheep (one-sixtieth, one-hundredth, one in 200) to fund the offerings. These are not tithes.

Ezekiel's calendar has a cleansing on the first day of the first month, Passover and Unleavened Bread, a seven-day festival in the seventh month (Booths), the Sabbath and the new moon. The Day of Atonement and the Feast of Weeks do not appear.

Ezekiel's Passover has no lamb and no family meal. On the fourteenth day the leader provides a bull as a sin offering for himself and the people, and a seven-day festival follows with seven bulls and seven rams daily.

sections.h: The Sabbath and the new moon at the east gate
sections.b: The east gate of the inner court is opened only on the Sabbath and the new moon; the leader and the people of the land bow down at it. The Sabbath offering is six lambs and a ram.

sections.h: The borders and the equal strips (47:13-48:29)
sections.b: Ezekiel's borders follow Numbers 34 in the north and south and use the Jordan for the east. The land is divided into twelve tribal strips, seven north of the holy district and five south of it, each the same, with the holy district between them. Whether they are to be read as a literal map, a promise or an ideal is disputed among Christians and Jews.

common: The strips do not match the old tribal land.

sections.b: The tribes are laid in strips from Dan in the north to Gad in the south, with Judah and Benjamin on either side of the sanctuary. Joseph counts twice (Ephraim and Manasseh). Levi gets no strip but a gate. The twelve gates of the city carry the tribes' names (48:31-34), and Revelation 21:12-13 uses the same pattern of three gates on each side.

sections.h: The city called 'The LORD Is There' (48:30-35)
sections.b: Ezekiel's city is a small square, 4,500 cubits on a side, with twelve gates named for the tribes and a new name, 'The LORD Is There'. It lies south of the Temple district and has no Temple of its own. Revelation 21 borrows the gates but makes the city a vast cube with no Temple at all.
Trees on both banks of the river bear fresh fruit every month and have leaves that heal, because the water flows from the sanctuary (47:12). Revelation 22:2 takes up the image for the tree of life.

The river's water 'heals' the Dead Sea so that fish live in it and fishermen stand along its shore. The same verb is used of Elisha healing the spring of Jericho (2 Kings 2:19-22). The leaves of the trees by the river are for healing too.
Ezekiel's river rises in the sanctuary, as Eden's rose in the garden (Genesis 2:10-14), and the trees by it recall the garden's. The pictures of a restored Eden are in Ezekiel 36:35 and 47:1-12.

The ruler of Ezekiel's restored land is called the leader, not the king. He sits in the east gate to eat before the LORD (44:3), supplies the festival offerings (45:17), worships at the gate (46:2) and holds land on both sides of the holy district (45:7; 48:21). He may not take the people's land (46:18) and the priests do the offering. The role is smaller than the king's in Kings.

sections.h: The glory fills the house again (44:4)
sections.b: Ezekiel sees the glory of the LORD fill the Temple a second time and falls on his face. The shut east gate (44:2) is the mark of its entry. The book closes with the city's name, 'The LORD Is There' (48:35).

Ezekiel's priests change clothes and cook the offerings in the priests' own rooms so that holiness does not spread to the people. The district is 'most holy' at its center, and the city beside it is 'common' (48:15).

sections.h: No Day of Atonement in Ezekiel
sections.b: Ezekiel 45:18-20 has a cleansing of the sanctuary on the first day of the first month and on a second day (the seventh of the month in the Hebrew, the first of the seventh month in Swete's Greek), but Leviticus 16's Day of Atonement does not appear. The Talmud records that Rabbi Yochanan thought Elijah would explain it.

sections.h: The year of release in Ezekiel 46:17
sections.b: A leader's gift of land to a servant lasts only until the year of release, the Jubilee. The principle is that land stays in the family that holds it.
The festival on the fifteenth of the seventh month is Booths, though Ezekiel does not name it. It gets the same offerings as Passover week.
The offerings the leader supplies make atonement for the house of Israel (45:15, 17); the sanctuary is cleansed with the blood of a sin offering (45:18-20).

A priest may be made unclean for a close relative only, then waits seven days and offers a sin offering. Priests teach the people the difference between clean and unclean (44:23) and do not eat what has died on its own or been torn (44:31).

Dispensationalist writers place Ezekiel's Temple, sacrifices and river in a future thousand-year reign of Christ; Reformed amillennial writers read them as pictures of the Church and of Christ's work; Catholic and Orthodox readers have used them for the Church and its worship. The sections on the sacrifices (44-46) are the center of the dispute.
